solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Book magazine for mature audience runs out of merchandise

indicators.note: out of is read here as outside of: the magazine and runs wrap around the merchandise

parts.note: The Oldie is a British monthly magazine aimed at older readers
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A magazine for older readers runs out of stock.
explanation.walkthrough: The magazine is a British monthly for older readers. 'Out of' is read as outside: the magazine plus the runs letter wraps round the merchandise word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ford Madox Ford's 1915 novel about two couples is the book meant.

clue.text: Eccentric president introduces advantageous measure

indicators.note: the president comes first and introduces the eccentric

parts.note: a card = an eccentric or comic person

explanation.surface: An odd head of state brings in a policy that benefits someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eccentric' reads as an adjective describing the president, but it is a noun, CARD, placed after him.
explanation.definitionFit: A trump card is a resource or move that gives you the advantage.

clue.text: One demanding money from former company employee

parts.note: an actor is employed by a theatre company

explanation.surface: Someone extorting cash from a man who used to work at the firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Company' suggests a business, but here it is a theatre company, whose employee is an actor.
explanation.definitionFit: An exactor is one who exacts, i.e. demands payment.

clue.text: Religious group summons state of harmony

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a monastic brotherhood, such as the Benedictines or Franciscans
second meaning: a noun here, a summons being an official command to appear in court
third meaning: peace and tidiness, everything in its proper place, as in law and peace

explanation.surface: A religious community calls everyone together to bring about peace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Summons' reads as a verb with the group as its subject, but it is a noun: a court summons is an order.
explanation.definitionFit: One word covers all three senses: a monastic brotherhood, a command to attend, and calm, regulated arrangement.

clue.text: Diligent editor in charge of obsolete presses

indicators.note: the obsolete word presses the editor and charge between its letters, holding them inside

explanation.surface: A hardworking editor runs some antiquated printing presses.
explanation.definitionFit: A dedicated worker is committed and conscientious, so diligent is a synonym.

clue.text: Former blonde wanting bleach primarily for new style

indicators.note: giving the letters a new style means rearranging them
wanting means lacking, so a letter is taken out of the word blonde
primarily picks the first letter of bleach

explanation.surface: A one-time blonde who gave up bleaching her hair in favour of a fresh look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanting' removes B, the first letter of bleach ('primarily'), from BLONDE, leaving LONDE, which 'for new style' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Olden is an old-fashioned adjective for bygone, as in the olden days, so it means former.

clue.text: Notice society girl in The Face

indicators.note: society and girl go inside the face

parts.note: dial = face, slang (and a clock face); split DI…AL

explanation.surface: An instruction to spot a debutante featured in The Face, a fashion magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notice' reads as a verb, but the definition is the noun, as in being given your notice. The Face was a British style magazine; dial is slang for face.
explanation.definitionFit: Being given notice means being dismissed from a job.

clue.text: Great rapper failing to hold last note regularly

indicators.note: failing to hold on to the final letter, so the rapper's name loses its end
regularly takes every other letter of note

parts.note: its alternate letters are N and T

explanation.surface: A star rapper whose voice cracks on the final note of a song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'failing to hold last' cuts the final M off EMINEM to give EMINE; 'regularly' then gives NT, the first and third letters of note.
explanation.definitionFit: An eminent person is distinguished and celebrated, which is what great means of a figure in history.

clue.text: Faculty originally translated nunc est bibendum the wrong way

indicators.note: read the letters backwards
take the first letter of each word

parts.note: first letters of translated, nunc, est, bibendum

explanation.surface: A university department mistranslates Horace's Latin 'now is the time for drinking'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faculty' suggests a university department, but here it means a natural talent. Nunc est bibendum is from Horace: 'now we must drink'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bent is a natural aptitude, a faculty for something.

clue.text: University backed faculty boss checking papers without staff?

indicators.note: the boss checks the papers, holding them in, so they sit inside
backed means turned round, so the boss is read backwards

parts.note: a dean heads a university faculty

explanation.surface: A university dean is reviewing someone's documents and seems short of support staff.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful sense of staff: not employees but a supporting stick.
explanation.definitionFit: Unaided means without help; staff can be people helping or a walking stick, so either way the support is absent.

clue.text: Intend secret to be kept from family

indicators.note: the family is kept away from, i.e. removed from, the secret

parts.note: clan = family, removed from the front

explanation.surface: A secret that must not be told to the relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a family secret; the family, CLAN, sits literally inside the word for secret.
explanation.definitionFit: To destine is to intend or set apart for a purpose.

clue.text: Safe seat finally accepted by member of House of Lords

indicators.note: accepted by says the letter goes inside the word for the Lords member

parts.note: a peer sits in the UK's House of Lords

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of seat

explanation.surface: A lord takes up a guaranteed seat in Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Safe' looks like an adjective for a secure seat, but it is the noun: peter is old criminal slang for a safe.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter is underworld slang for a strongbox, as in a peterman, a safe-breaker.

clue.text: Bold study reflected uncertainty and evidence of impact

indicators.note: the word for uncertainty is mirrored

parts.note: an if = a doubt; reflected to FI
a dent shows where something hit

explanation.surface: A daring piece of research shows doubt and the marks left by a collision.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reflected' reads as 'showed' with study, but it works on the word after it, reversing IF.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a bold manner and a confident one both show no fear of failing.

clue.text: Mad race around island involves flying boat performing stunts

indicators.note: the scrambled race goes around the rest, so the other letters sit inside it
involves says the boat and island are taken inside the race
mad suggests the letters of race are crazily rearranged
flying suggests the letters of boat are thrown about into a new order

explanation.surface: A frantic race around an island includes a flying boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad' scrambles race, and the scrambled letters go around both the scrambled boat and the island.
explanation.definitionFit: Aerobatic describes the loops and rolls an aircraft does in a display, which are stunts.

clue.text: Associate academic finishes teaching course

indicators.note: the academic finishes, i.e. comes at the end of, the teaching course

explanation.surface: A junior lecturer completes a teacher-training course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Associate academic' looks like a job title; Associate is the definition, and BEd is the British teaching degree.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedfellow is an associate or ally, as in 'strange bedfellows'.

clue.text: Firm sanctioned about member involved in dodgy deals?

indicators.note: firm and sanctioned sit about, i.e. around, the member

explanation.surface: A company given official approval over an MP, amid hints of shady dealings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sanctioned' can mean penalised, which suits the dodgy deals, but here it means approved: LICIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: shady dealing is one kind of wrongdoing a complicit person takes part in, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Television also broadcast fight

indicators.note: spoken, so 'too' can stand for its sound-alike

explanation.surface: A TV network also airs a boxing match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' fits the television, but it is the sound instruction on 'also'.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal British idiom: a set-to is a brief scrap or heated quarrel.

clue.text: Overcomes unacceptable methods of Speaker

indicators.note: words 'of a speaker' are heard rather than read, so the answer only sounds like the phrase

explanation.surface: Someone defeats the Speaker's improper procedures in the Commons.
explanation.walkthrough: The Speaker suggests the House of Commons, but it just means the words are spoken. 'Out' means not acceptable, as in 'that's out'.
explanation.definitionFit: To outweigh is to be greater than, to overcome.

clue.text: Gave drugs to note first signs of side effects directly

parts.note: do (or doh) is the first note of the sol-fa scale

indicators.note: first signs of takes the opening letter of each following word

parts.note: their first letters are S, E and D

explanation.surface: A doctor's report on a medicine whose side effects showed up at once.
explanation.walkthrough: DO is the sol-fa note, as in do-re-mi; 'first signs of' takes S, E and D from side effects directly.
explanation.definitionFit: To dose someone is to give them a measured amount of medicine.

clue.text: Benefit surrounding success mushrooms

definitions.note: plural in the clue: shitake is used as a plural too

indicators.note: the benefit goes round the success

parts.note: for the sake of = for the benefit of; split S…AKE

explanation.surface: A charity event around a hit show, perhaps selling mushrooms.
explanation.walkthrough: This spelling, SHITAKE, is a less common variant of shiitake, the Japanese mushroom.
explanation.definitionFit: Shiitake, also spelt shitake, are Japanese edible mushrooms.

clue.text: Childhood implies those cases presenting as most depressed superficially?

indicators.note: the phrase holds the answer in its casing and presents it

explanation.surface: A pediatric study suggests which cases seem most seriously depressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depressed' suggests mood, but the question mark signals the literal sense: a dimple is a small dent in the surface of the skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Dimpliest means having the most dimples, the most small hollows on the surface.

clue.text: Opening of epic Gaelic novel written in verse form

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter
novel means new, so the letters of Gaelic take a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: The start of an Irish epic, set down as a new work of fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book beside 'epic', but it means new, the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Elegiac verse uses the elegiac couplet, a classical metre, so the word names a poetic form of writing.

clue.text: Union member doing fine in correctional facility

parts.note: one member of a marriage union

explanation.surface: A trade union member is getting on fine in prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Union' suggests a trade union; it is a marriage. Bridewell was a London prison, and the name became a general word for a jail.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridewell is a house of correction, a jail.

clue.text: Flyers typically seen in night clubs

definitions.meaning: clubs for hitting a ball, as in cricket or baseball

explanation.surface: Party animals usually spotted in nightclubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Night clubs' reads as one place to go dancing; it splits into the end of the first definition and a second.
explanation.definitionFit: Bats fly at night, and bats are clubs used to hit a ball.

clue.text: English nation turning strangely frightening

indicators.note: the nation is written backwards

explanation.surface: An English country growing oddly scary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strangely' looks like an anagram indicator, but it belongs to the definition; the turning is a plain reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the whole phrase: eerie fear is the uncanny kind, frightening because it is strange.

clue.text: Important piece of music that man encountered when cycling

indicators.note: the last letter moves round to the front

explanation.surface: A tune a man happened upon while out on his bike.
explanation.walkthrough: HEMET cycled, with its final T brought to the front, gives THEME.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is the main melody a piece is built on, so its most important part.

clue.text: What may be used to flog waste ground

definitions.text: What may be used to flog

indicators.note: waste is ground up, broken down

explanation.surface: A whip for sale found on a patch of wasteland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waste ground' is a phrase for derelict land; 'ground' is the anagram indicator. A tawse is a Scottish leather strap once used to punish schoolchildren. 'Flog' can mean sell as well as beat.
explanation.definitionFit: A tawse is a leather strap used for beating.

clue.text: Advertisement reinvented retail therapy essentially

indicators.note: the essence, the middle letter, of therapy

explanation.surface: An advert for a new take on shopping as a mood-lifter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retail therapy' is a set phrase for shopping to cheer up; the words split between anagram fodder and a middle letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A trailer is an advertisement for a forthcoming film or programme.

clue.text: Threatening to incarcerate Liberal in protective housing

explanation.surface: Politicians menacing to lock up a Liberal inside a secure building.
explanation.walkthrough: A cowling is the removable cover over an engine.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowling is a protective metal cover housing an engine.

clue.text: Novel exploit restricted to most of these hosts

parts.note: something restricted to two parties is between them, as in between you and me

indicators.note: the shortened word hosts the exploit, holding it inside
most of the word means its last letter is dropped

parts.note: an exploit is a deed or act

explanation.surface: A novel trick is reserved for most of the hosts present.
explanation.walkthrough: THESE loses its last letter to make THES, which holds ACT to give THEACTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Between the Acts is the final novel by Virginia Woolf, published in 1941.
